chapter_title: Object Placement and Manipulation in AR

screens.title: Object Placement and Manipulation in AR
screens.subtitle: How raycasting, spawning, and touch gestures let users place and change virtual objects convincingly.

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on the core skills you need to place and manipulate virtual objects so they feel anchored to the real world. You will learn the role of raycasting to find precise placement points, how to spawn and manage prefabs at runtime, and how to let users move, scale, or rotate objects with touch gestures. These building blocks are essential because a believable AR scene depends on accurate hits, consistent object state, and predictable interactions. For example, a misplaced chair will immediately break immersion; by using the ARRaycastManager to obtain a pose and instantiate a prefab at the returned position and rotation, you achieve much better alignment with floors and tables. We will also look at common problems like object drift and scale perception and practical steps to test and reduce them. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to implement a single-object placement flow, add a one-finger drag for translation, and prepare for adding anchors to improve stability in the next chapter. Consider how users will expect objects to remain steady and how touch behavior should feel natural — that focus will guide your implementation decisions.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Use raycasts to get precise Pose data, instantiate prefabs at that Pose, and provide intuitive touch gestures for translation, scaling, and rotation while watching for drift and perceptual errors.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter — practical skills and tested milestones.

narration.text: Over the next screens you will acquire four interlocking competencies that let you place and interact with virtual objects in AR. First, you will implement raycasting with AR Foundation so touches reliably find a valid placement Pose on detected planes. This matters because accurate Pose data is the basis for believable alignment. Second, you will dynamically spawn 3D models by instantiating prefabs at runtime and manage those instances for future manipulation. That skill ensures your app can create content when and where the user needs it. Third, you will implement responsive touch handling so users can translate, rotate, and scale objects using single- and multi-touch gestures. This improves usability and makes interactions feel natural. Fourth, you will learn to identify and mitigate common problems like object drift and poor scale perception through testing strategies and simple visual cues. Each objective includes a verified competency milestone so you and your learners can confirm practical competence on a device.

screens.title: Raycasting — mapping touch to world Pose
screens.subtitle: How a screen tap becomes a precise position and rotation in Unity AR.

narration.text: Raycasting is the mechanism that turns a 2D touch coordinate into a 3D intersection with the environment. In AR Foundation you use the ARRaycastManager to project a virtual ray from the screen point into the session and request trackable hits. When the ray intersects a detected plane it returns a Pose object — a position and a rotation in Unity world space — that tells you exactly where and how a virtual object should be placed. This is more than a single coordinate: the Pose encodes orientation relative to the plane, so your model can align naturally with floor or table normals. A common misconception is that raycasting alone makes an object stable forever. In reality, a raycast provides a snapshot hit at placement time; ongoing tracking and anchors determine long-term stability. Concrete example: when the user taps a tabletop, call arRaycastManager. Raycast(touch. position, hits, TrackableType. PlaneWithinPolygon). If hits has entries, use hits[0]. pose to place or move your object. Why this matters: accurate Pose data is the difference between a convincing AR object that appears to rest on a surface and a floating or clipped model. As you implement raycasting, log the Pose position and rotation values during testing so you can spot misalignments early and adjust how you orient the prefab on placement.

keyIdea.title: Raycasting insight
keyIdea.text: A raycast converts touch into a Pose — position plus rotation — which is the canonical placement anchor for spawned objects.

content.html:
Core Concept
Raycasting
Definition: project a ray from a screen point to detect intersections with AR trackables and receive a Pose for placement.
Why it matters
  • Provides exact world coordinates so objects rest naturally on surfaces.
  • Delivers rotation information so prefabs align with plane normals.
  • Forms the foundation for spawning and manipulation logic.
Common misconception
Raycasts are a placement snapshot, not a permanence guarantee; anchors or other stability tools are needed to maintain placement over time.
Key Takeaway

Use ARRaycastManager to get Pose data—position and rotation—then instantiate or move objects at that Pose.

Raycast example (conceptual)
// Conceptual usage in AR Foundation
if (arRaycastManager.Raycast(touch.position, hits, TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon))
{
  Pose hitPose = hits[0].pose;
  // hitPose.position -> world position
  // hitPose.rotation -> surface-aligned rotation
}
Example: tap a table and receive a Pose with a rotation aligned to the table normal.
Debug tip: log position and rotation to inspect misalignments during testing.
Analogy: think of the ray as a laser pointer from the camera through the touch point; the Pose is where that laser first hits a real surface and how it sits there.

screens.title: Using ARRaycastManager and reading the Pose
screens.subtitle: Practical pattern for raycasting, hit results, and Pose extraction.

narration.text: When you wire up placement, the ARRaycastManager is the central A P I for hitting trackables. The standard pattern is to cache a List of ARRaycastHit results, call arRaycastManager. Raycast with the touch screen position and a TrackableType filter such as PlaneWithinPolygon, and then inspect hits[0]. pose if the call returns true. The Pose gives you both position and rotation in world coordinates, which you pass directly to Instantiate when creating a new object. A useful convention is to perform this logic only when touch. phase indicates a beginning tap or during moved phases for continuous drag. A potential pitfall is calling Instantiate for every touch without preserving a reference; this quickly creates many objects. Instead, store a reference to the spawned GameObject when you want a single object, or keep a list if multiple placements are intended. In practice, developers also test whether hit poses are on the right plane by checking trackable IDs or plane alignment when required. Finally, log or visualize the Pose using a small marker prefab during development so you can see where hits land in the world and validate plane alignment before instantiating complex models.

keyIdea.title: ARRaycastManager pattern
keyIdea.text: Raycast into the session, read hits[0].pose, and use that Pose to instantiate or update GameObject transforms.

content.html:
Process
ARRaycastManager Workflow
Step-by-step: perform a raycast, check results, extract the Pose, then instantiate or move an object.
1. Check Input.touchCount and touch.phase to know when to raycast.
2. Call arRaycastManager.Raycast(touch.position, hits, TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon).
3. If hits found, use hits[0].pose.position and .rotation for placement.
4. Store references to spawned objects to move or remove them later.
Code snippet (concept)
// Example pattern
if (arRaycastManager.Raycast(touch.position, hits, TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon))
{
  Pose hitPose = hits[0].pose;
  // Use hitPose.position and hitPose.rotation for placement
}
Example card: Use a tiny debug marker at the Pose when learning; this quick feedback confirms plane alignment and helps debug rotation issues before you spawn a final model.

screens.title: Instantiating prefabs at the hit Pose
screens.subtitle: Best practices for spawning and deciding single vs multiple placements.

narration.text: Instantiating a prefab at a Pose is the straightforward mapping from a raycast hit to visible content. Use Instantiate(objectToPlace, hitPose. position, hitPose. rotation) to create the object aligned to the surface. But beyond the call itself, you must decide how many objects you want and how to manage them. A common pattern is the single-object placement model: keep one placedObject reference, instantiate on the first tap, and on later taps move that same object. This avoids clutter and is suitable for apps where the user arranges a single item. Alternatively, allow multiple instantiations and store each created GameObject in a list for later editing or removal. Manage lifecycles explicitly: provide ways to delete or reset placed objects in your app flow. Also consider orientation adjustments: sometimes you want the object to face the camera after placement; in that case, adjust rotation after instantiation rather than relying solely on hitPose. rotation. Lastly, always test with your specific prefab: bounding volumes, pivot points, and scale inside the model affect how it sits on the plane. If a model sinks or floats, fix its pivot or apply a small Y offset on placement so the base rests correctly on the plane surface.

keyIdea.title: Instantiation tip
keyIdea.text: Call Instantiate with hitPose data, but manage instances and pivot/offsets so models sit naturally and user intentions are respected.

content.html:
Definition
Instantiate(prefab, position, rotation)
Decide if taps create a new object or move an existing one. Manage references and lists for later manipulation.
Single-object pattern avoids clutter and simplifies manipulation logic.
Multiple-object pattern requires lists and UI to select or delete objects.
Pivot and model bounds matter: adjust offsets if a model appears sunk or floating.
Concrete example
Place a chair prefab at hitPose; if the seat is below the plane, correct the prefab pivot or add a small upward offset before instantiating.
Example placement code
// Instantiate at the hit pose
GameObject newObj = Instantiate(objectToPlace, hitPose.position + Vector3.up * yOffset, hitPose.rotation);
// Optionally adjust rotation to face camera
newObj.transform.LookAt(cameraTransform.position);
Key takeaway: the Instantiate call is simple; the surrounding lifecycle management and model alignment determine whether placement feels polished.

screens.title: Managing spawned objects and selection
screens.subtitle: Patterns to store, move, and remove instantiated GameObjects.

narration.text: Once objects appear in the scene you need a clear architecture for managing them. A simple approach uses a single reference placedObject when you only want one active item. For multiple objects, create a managed list that stores each instantiated GameObject. Add lightweight helper methods: SpawnAtPose(Pose pose) to instantiate and register, MoveToPose(GameObject obj, Pose pose) to update transforms, and Remove(GameObject obj) to destroy and remove from the list. Selection is important: if users can manipulate many objects, provide a simple selection state so gestures apply to the intended object. A typical selection strategy is to perform a raycast from the touch into existing virtual objects (not into the AR session) to pick the nearest object, or to use a tap to toggle selection. Remember to separate placement raycasts (against trackables) from selection raycasts (against spawned colliders). Also keep your data structures clean: if you persist placed objects between sessions, record their poses and restore them thoughtfully, with a re-localization step to reduce drift. Concrete example: keep a List placedObjects; when instantiating push the new object onto the list; when deleting, call Destroy and remove it from the list. This predictable lifecycle reduces bugs and memory leaks as scenes grow.

keyIdea.title: Management pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a single reference or a managed list, separate selection from placement raycasts, and provide spawn/move/remove helpers for predictable lifecycle control.

content.html:
Process Flow
Object Management
Spawn, store, select, move, and remove with clear APIs and simple data structures.
SpawnAtPose: Instantiate and add to List<GameObject>.
MoveToPose: Update transform.position and rotation or use smooth interpolation for UX.
Remove: Destroy and remove from list to avoid leaks.
Select: Raycast against object colliders to pick which object a gesture should affect.
Example: keep a selectedObject variable. When a tap hits an object collider set selectedObject; then gestures modify that object rather than creating a new one.
Selection vs Placement
Placement raycasts target TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon. Selection raycasts test spawned object colliders. Keep these concerns separate to avoid placing when the user intended to select.
Concrete example
Tap once to place. Tap an object to select it. Then drag to move the selected object using plane raycasts during movement.

screens.title: One-finger drag for plane-based translation
screens.subtitle: Implementing continuous movement by raycasting during touch move phases.

narration.text: A one-finger drag that moves a placed object along a detected plane is a common and intuitive interaction. The pattern is straightforward: when there is a placedObject and Input. touchCount is one, on TouchPhase. Moved perform a plane raycast at the current finger position. If the raycast returns a hit, set placedObject. transform. position to the hitPose. position. This gives the feeling that the object is sliding across the surface as the user drags their finger. One subtlety is when to instantiate: typically you only instantiate on the initial TouchPhase. Began if the placedObject is null; on subsequent moved phases you should avoid instantiating and instead update the existing object. Another subtlety is smoothing: directly snapping the object to the hit position can feel choppy on some devices; using Vector3. Lerp to interpolate toward the hit position each frame can improve perceived responsiveness. Finally, remember to update rotation only when desired — you might want the object to maintain its original orientation or to align to hitPose. rotation depending on your UX goals. Test dragging across plane boundaries and ensure the object doesn't unexpectedly jump when the raycast target switches between planes.

keyIdea.title: Drag pattern
keyIdea.text: During TouchPhase.Moved, raycast and update the placed object's position to the hit Pose for smooth plane-aligned translation; consider interpolation to reduce choppiness.

content.html:
Process
One-finger Drag
Use TouchPhase.Moved + raycast to update the object's world position along the plane.
Instantiate only on first touch if no placedObject exists.
On moved, raycast and set placedObject.transform.position = hitPose.position.
Optional: smooth movement with Lerp to improve UX.
Common mistake: performing placement Instantiate inside moved logic, which spawns many objects. Only move the existing reference on moved phases.
Code (conceptual)
// On TouchPhase.Moved
if (arRaycastManager.Raycast(touch.position, hits, TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon))
{
  Pose hitPose = hits[0].pose;
  placedObject.transform.position = Vector3.Lerp(placedObject.transform.position, hitPose.position, 0.6f);
}
UX tip: tune the lerp factor for responsiveness. Too low feels laggy; too high can feel jittery on noisy tracking.

screens.title: Multi-touch gestures: pinch to scale and twist to rotate
screens.subtitle: High-level steps to detect two-finger gestures and apply smooth transformations.

narration.text: Two-finger gestures let users control scale and rotation. The high-level approach is to detect when Input. touchCount equals two, then track distance and angle between the two touches. On TouchPhase. Began for both touches, record the initial distance between touch positions and the current localScale of the object as initialScale. While TouchPhase. Moved occurs for either touch, compute the current distance and derive a scaleFactor as currentDistance divided by initialDistance, then set placedObject. transform. localScale = initialScale * scaleFactor. For rotation, record the initial angle between the two touch vectors on begin, then on moved compute the current angle and apply the delta to the object's rotation around the appropriate axis. A common mistake is applying absolute touches instead of deltas, which can cause jumps when fingers briefly lift. Another is failing to clamp scale: impose reasonable min and max localScale values to prevent objects becoming impractically large or inverted. In practice, combine scaling and rotation handling so simultaneous pinch-and-rotate gestures feel natural. Remember to store initial values at gesture start so transformations are relative and smooth. This approach keeps interactions predictable and aligns with common mobile UX expectations.

keyIdea.title: Gesture steps
keyIdea.text: Record initial distance and angle at gesture start, compute scaleFactor and angle delta while moving, and apply changes with clamping for stable, predictable results.

content.html:
Process
Pinch & Twist Gestures
Detect two touches, store initial distance and angle, then apply relative transforms during move phases.
Step 1: On two-touch begin store initialDistance and initialScale.
Step 2: On moved compute currentDistance and scaleFactor = current / initial.
Step 3: Apply rotation delta from the change in angle between touch vectors.
Step 4: Clamp localScale to a safe min/max range to protect UX.
High-level pseudocode
// On two-finger begin
initialDistance = Distance(touch0.pos, touch1.pos)
initialScale = placedObject.transform.localScale
initialAngle = AngleBetween(touch0, touch1)

// On moved
currentDistance = Distance(touch0.pos, touch1.pos)
scaleFactor = currentDistance / initialDistance
placedObject.transform.localScale = initialScale * scaleFactor

currentAngle = AngleBetween(touch0, touch1)
angleDelta = currentAngle - initialAngle
placedObject.transform.Rotate(0, -angleDelta, 0)
UX note: tune sensitivity so small finger jitter doesn't trigger large changes; use smoothing or dead zones as needed.

screens.title: Object drift — causes and practical checks
screens.subtitle: Understand what makes objects slide and how to reproduce and diagnose it.

narration.text: Object drift is when a placed object slowly shifts from its intended real-world location. It's a frustrating user experience because the object loses its perceived permanence. Two common contributing factors are environmental conditions and user motion. Poor environmental conditions mean few distinct visual features: a plain floor, low texture, very bright or dim lighting, or reflective surfaces make SLAM and feature tracking less reliable. Rapid or jerky device movement can also cause tracking to momentarily fail and produce cumulative positional error. To diagnose drift reproducibly, test in controlled environments: try a textured scene versus a featureless floor, change lighting levels, and walk around while observing the object. Log camera pose updates and the object's world position over time to quantify drift. Short-term mitigations include encouraging users to avoid sudden movements, adding AR Anchors when available, and designing UX that tolerates small shifts—such as using slight visual smoothing or offering a reset action. A common misconception is that drift indicates a bug in placement code; often it is a limitation of the environment or the current tracking state. Understanding these differences helps you choose whether to change code, improve testing conditions, or plan for anchors in the next chapter.

keyIdea.title: Drift diagnosis
keyIdea.text: Drift usually stems from tracking limits or poor environmental features; reproduce with controlled tests and use anchors or UX mitigations to reduce its impact.

content.html:
Comparison
Drift Causes vs Symptoms
Cause: Poor visual features (plain floors, low texture)
Cause: Rapid, jerky device motion that breaks SLAM tracking
Symptom: Object slowly slides despite the device being held still
Symptom: Sudden jumps when relocalization occurs
Diagnosis & Mitigation
  • Reproduce drift by walking around the object and varying lighting.
  • Log positions over time to quantify movement and find correlations.
  • Mitigate with anchors, UX resets, or by instructing users to move slowly.
  • Design tests in different environments to understand limits.
Common mistake

Assuming drift is always code-related; often it is environmental or tracking-limit related. Test before refactoring placement logic.

screens.title: Scale perception and visual cues
screens.subtitle: Techniques to help users judge object size in mixed reality.

narration.text: Scale perception is the user's ability to judge how big a virtual object is relative to the real world. In AR this can be surprisingly difficult because the user lacks consistent reference points. To improve perception, provide visual cues that give context: a grid on the detected plane, a small reference object of known physical size, or a shadow that matches the object's base. These cues provide anchors for human perception and reduce uncertainty about whether a model is life-sized or miniaturized. Another technique is to supply interactive labels or overlays indicating approximate real-world dimensions. A common misconception is that simply scaling the object to a value that 'looks right' on one device will work for all devices; testing across different cameras and lighting conditions is essential because apparent size varies with device field of view and user distance. In practice, add a toggle to show or hide a reference marker during placement, and test with a colleague holding a real object of known size to calibrate perceived scale. These small affordances make it easier for users to place and accept objects in their environment and reduce errors when arranging scenes.

keyIdea.title: Perception tip
keyIdea.text: Provide consistent real-world reference cues—grids, reference objects, or shadows—to help users accurately judge virtual object size.

content.html:
Definition
Scale Perception
Help users judge size with visual context and reference objects.
Grid overlay on plane to show units and spacing.
Reference object of known size (e.g., a coin or ruler model).
Soft shadow under object to ground it visually.
Concrete checks
  • Toggle a reference model and compare against a held real object.
  • Test in wide and narrow FOV devices to ensure consistent perception.
  • Offer an optional label that reports approximate real-world dimensions.
Key Takeaway

Small visual cues greatly improve user confidence when judging virtual object size.

screens.title: Safety, permissions, and testing best practices
screens.subtitle: Design choices and test strategies to build robust, safe AR experiences.

narration.text: AR apps must be tested and designed with both safety and permission handling in mind. First, always request camera permissions gracefully and explain why camera access is required. On iOS and Android provide a short, clear rationale before prompting so users understand the need. Second, design interactions that minimize unsafe behavior: avoid long sessions that force users to look down continuously, provide visual and textual prompts to be aware of surroundings, and avoid placing tasks that require walking blindly while focused on the screen. For testing, exercise a variety of real-world conditions: bright sunlight, dim indoor lighting, reflective surfaces, and large open spaces. These variations reveal tracking edge cases such as lost plane detection or increased drift. Include automated logging in debug builds for Pose and tracking state so you can correlate issues with environmental conditions. Finally, run user trials to observe how people naturally try to interact; their patterns will reveal whether your gestures are discoverable and whether placement semantics match expectations. These pragmatic steps help you ship safer, more reliable AR experiences. Safety, permissions, and testing best practices means request permissions clearly, design for user awareness of the real world, and test across lighting and surface conditions to detect tracking limits.. In practical terms, design choices and test strategies to build robust, safe ar experiences.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safety & testing
keyIdea.text: Request permissions clearly, design for user awareness of the real world, and test across lighting and surface conditions to detect tracking limits.

content.html:
Definition
Permissions & Safety
Explain camera access, encourage situational awareness, and avoid interactions that distract users from obstacles.
Prompt with rationale before requesting camera permission.
Provide visual reminders to watch surroundings during active AR sessions.
Avoid UX that forces continuous downward focus in hazardous environments.
Testing checklist
  • Run in bright sunlight, dim rooms, and high-reflectivity areas.
  • Log Pose and tracking state in debug builds for postmortem analysis.
  • Perform user trials to validate gesture discoverability and placement expectations.
Key Takeaway

Real-world testing across conditions is essential; permissions and safety prompts protect users and reduce support issues.

screens.title: Lab: Modify ARPlacementManager and add drag translation
screens.subtitle: Walkthrough of code changes to create single-object placement and one-finger drag.

narration.text: This hands-on activity guides you through modifying ARPlacementManager to implement single-object placement and a simple drag translation. Start by opening your existing ARPlacementManager. cs and ensure you have an ARRaycastManager reference and a List<ARRaycastHit> for results. Add a private GameObject placedObject to hold the single instance. In Awake cache the ARRaycastManager. In Update, check Input. touchCount and get the first touch. For touch began, attempt a raycast. If no placedObject exists and the raycast hit, instantiate your prefab at hits[0]. pose. If placedObject already exists, then during TouchPhase. Moved perform another raycast and update placedObject. transform. position to the new hitPose. position so the object follows the finger. This pattern keeps instantiation only on the initial tap and uses moved phases to translate. After implementing, build to device and test: the first tap should create the cube; dragging should move it; subsequent taps should move it as well. If you observe jumps, add smoothing using Lerp. This exercise consolidates the chapter's key skills: raycasting, instantiation, stateful object management, and touch-driven translation. Lab: Modify ARPlacementManager and add drag translation means implement single-object placement and one-finger drag by instantiating once and using moved-phase raycasts to update the object's position.. In practical terms, walkthrough of code changes to create single-object placement and one-finger drag.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Lab focus
keyIdea.text: Implement single-object placement and one-finger drag by instantiating once and using moved-phase raycasts to update the object's position.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Modify ARPlacementManager
Follow these steps: add a placedObject reference, cache ARRaycastManager in Awake, use Begin for initial instantiate, use Moved for translation updates.
Step 1: Open ARPlacementManager and add private GameObject placedObject.
Step 2: In Update, on TouchPhase.Began raycast and instantiate if placedObject is null.
Step 3: On TouchPhase.Moved raycast and set placedObject.transform.position to hitPose.position.
Step 4: Build to device and test first tap = place, drag = move.
Starter code (from chapter)
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARFoundation;
using UnityEngine.XR.ARSubsystems;
using System.Collections.Generic;

public class ARPlacementManager : MonoBehaviour
{
    [SerializeField] private GameObject objectToPlace; // Assign your ARCubeprefab here
    private ARRaycastManager arRaycastManager;
    private static List hits = new List();

    private GameObject placedObject; // Reference to the currently placed object

    void Awake()
    {
        arRaycastManager = GetComponent();
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (Input.touchCount > 0)
        {
            Touch touch = Input.GetTouch(0);

            // Handle initial placement or moving existing object
            if (touch.phase == TouchPhase.Began || touch.phase == TouchPhase.Moved)
            {
                if (arRaycastManager.Raycast(touch.position, hits, TrackableType.PlaneWithinPolygon))
                {
                    Pose hitPose = hits[0].pose;

                    if (placedObject == null)
                    {
                        // On first touch, if no object exists, instantiate it
                        if (touch.phase == TouchPhase.Began) // Only instantiate on the very first touch
                        {
                            placedObject = Instantiate(objectToPlace, hitPose.position, hitPose.rotation);
                        }
                    }
                    else
                    {
                        // If an object exists, move it to the new hit position
                        placedObject.transform.position = hitPose.position;
                        // Optional: Adjust rotation if you want it to always face the camera or align with the plane
                        // placedObject.transform.rotation = hitPose.rotation;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
Build and run: first tap places the cube, subsequent taps or drags move it. Add Lerp to smooth movement if needed.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Core terms and short explanations to recall quickly.

narration.text: Here are the essential concepts to remember when placing and manipulating AR objects. Raycasting projects a virtual ray from a touch point into the session to find trackable intersections and returns a Pose with position and rotation. Dynamic spawning refers to instantiating prefabs at runtime using the hit Pose, and managing those instances lets you move, remove, or update objects later.
